mount-cache choosing how the guest caches the project folder’s mount, which devvm mount-cache sets native on Linux, where it’s 9p’s cache option, none for new VMs (details). None on macOS, where virtiofs has no such option
agent-folders agents’ host folders, read-only native: read-only mounts, enforced by the host
tools-share the shared tools, read-only native: a read-only mount, enforced by the host
egress-proxy network traffic only through devvm’s proxy native: Seatbelt on macOS, and on Linux QEMU’s restrict=on with a guestfwd to the proxy (details)
ssh ssh for editors native: Lima’s ssh forward and config
ports the listed ports forwarded to the host’s loopback emulated (reviewed): devvm’s forwarder over Lima’s ssh, for the listed ports alone, with Lima’s own forwards off (details)
ports-all every port forwarded, servers on the VM’s loopback included emulated (reviewed): the same forwarder, for whatever listens in the VM from port 1024 up, and never a port the host has (details)
agent-forwarding ssh-agent forwarding, chosen when the VM is made native
agent-toggle turning a VM’s ssh-agent forwarding on or off later native
cpus a VM’s CPUs native
memory a VM’s memory native
disk a VM’s disk size native: it grows but never shrinks
docker-layer the docker layer: Docker’s engine running in the VM native
nix-layer the nix layer: Nix’s daemon and its store in the VM, with builds in Nix’s sandbox native (details)
link links between VMs: a program in one VM reaches a port another VM publishes, by name native: a link session of devvm’s own over Lima’s ssh, with remote forwards to 127.77.0.0/16 alone (details)

egress-proxy is what every network tier but open needs. The open tier needs no feature of its own: every backend must let a VM on its own network (NetDirect) reach a port on the host’s loopback and set the guest’s proxy settings from the confinement (Confinement.GuestProxy, ProxyURL), which the conformance suite checks (checkProxyURL), because every VM’s proxy carries its requests. So a backend without egress-proxy still has open VMs, and devvm refuses every other tier on it in one line (net_tier_backend).

What each backend emulates

On Lima, devvm emulates forwarding ports, both the listed ones and every one, through its forwarder, and the emulation is reviewed (port forwarding). Everything else on Lima is Lima’s own.

The forwarder is devvm’s own on every backend, never a backend’s. A backend that has ports turns its own forwards off, and devvm’s forwarder reaches a running VM’s sshd the way the backend’s SSH says, which is a user, a key and a port. devvm refuses that target unless it’s on this machine’s loopback, 127.0.0.1, with the same check it uses for links and the ssh config (vmssh.FromTarget). devvm reads which ports the VM forwards from its state, chooses which of them are free, pins the VM’s host keys for its current start and starts the forwarder, which follows the backend’s lifeline for the VM.

Missing and unreviewed features

devvm checks each feature an image or a VM needs this way:

flowchart TD
need["a feature the image<br>or the VM needs"] --> how{{"how the backend has it"}}
how -- "native" --> ok["allowed"]
how -- "emulated, reviewed" --> ok
how -- "emulated, unreviewed,<br>or none" --> np{{"egress-proxy, for<br>a new open VM?"}}
np -- "no" --> refused["refused: devvm stops<br>and names the VM,<br>the feature and the backend"]
np -- "yes" --> warned["the VM is made open,<br>as asked"]

Before devvm builds an image, makes or starts a VM, or changes a VM’s settings, it checks that the backend has every feature the image or the VM needs. The backend itself is behind the same check: every time devvm asks it to build an image or the shared tools, make a VM or start one, devvm checks the features that request needs before the backend sees it, so a request that skipped the first check is refused too. When the backend lacks one, devvm stops and names the VM, the feature and the backend (backend_lacks). It does the same for a feature the backend only emulates when that emulation’s review hasn’t passed (backend_unreviewed). devvm never falls back to something weaker, so a VM on a confined tier never starts with an open network.

To get the feature, use a backend that has it. A VM keeps its backend, so that means making a new VM.

A new VM’s tier is the one exception, because allowlist is the default, and When a backend lacks something says what devvm does instead.

What a start changes

A backend makes a VM as devvm asks, and then changes it only when it starts. Each time devvm starts a stopped VM, it tells the backend what the VM’s state asks for, which is its size, the agent folders in devvm’s agent store and whether it forwards your SSH agent, together with how the VM is confined. The backend compares that with the VM it has and changes only what differs, so a start that changes nothing leaves the VM’s config as it was. Nothing changes a stopped VM’s config between starts, so devvm size and devvm ssh-agent save what you ask for in the VM’s state, and the VM gets it when it next starts.

A running VM is left as it is, and devvm says what changes when it next starts. Its ports aren’t the backend’s, so devvm ports changes them at once, and a running VM’s forwarder starts again with the new ones (port forwarding). A disk can’t shrink, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before the backend changes anything (disk_shrink).

Which ports a VM forwards stays in the VM’s state alone, and the backend never hears of them. The backend keeps only what it needs for the start it made, such as Lima’s record of the hostagent it started confined (confinement).

VM names

A project VM’s name is devvm-<folder>-<hash>. The folder part is up to 20 characters of the folder’s name, in lowercase, with characters other than letters and digits turned into dashes, and the hash part is 14 hex digits of a hash of the folder’s path. devvm takes a name as a project VM’s only when it has that form, so a name in a state file or a backend’s list whose folder part has any other character, or starts or ends with a dash, isn’t a project VM’s.

A backend may need shorter names, and then devvm cuts the folder’s part to fit. When fewer than 4 characters of it would fit, devvm refuses (vm_name_no_room). On Lima the room for a name depends on the Lima home’s path, because Lima keeps each VM’s ssh socket under it, so there the fix is a shorter Lima home (lima_home_too_long, limits).

Only a new VM gets a name, which fits the limit of the backend that makes it. devvm finds a folder’s VM by the state that records the folder’s path, in the VM’s folder in devvm’s data folder (vms/<hash>/, named by the hash that ends the VM’s name), so an existing VM keeps the name and the backend its state records, whichever backend new VMs get, and keeps them when its folder moves (a moved folder).

Which backends a launch asks

A launch asks a backend about its VMs only when some VM’s state names that backend. It asks them to write the ssh config and to check the SSH agent’s folders. So a backend that no VM uses never runs during a launch, even when it isn’t running or isn’t installed (a VM’s backend).

item.title: Lima
item.description:
This page explains how devvm runs its VMs on Lima: the Lima home it keeps them in, how it builds images and clones VMs from them, what it sets in each VM’s config, how it confines VMs and builds, and how it forwards their ports. Lima covers what you need to run it, devvm limactl and Lima’s limits.

A Lima home of its own

Lima merges _config/default.yaml and _config/override.yaml from its home into every VM it creates or starts. A network you set there for your own VMs would give a devvm VM a second network card with a route around its proxy, and an extra mount set there would go unnoticed. So devvm keeps its VMs in a Lima home of their own, ~/.local/share/devvm/lima, whatever LIMA_HOME says (devvm’s Lima home says what that means for you).

devvm refuses to start a VM while that home holds either file (lima_global_config), and it refuses a VM that has a network devvm didn’t give it (vm_has_networks).

devvm runs limactl from its own data folder. When a config is invalid, Lima writes lima.REJECTED.yaml into the folder it runs in, and a project folder belongs to the VM to write.

Clones and overlays

An image is a stopped VM in devvm’s Lima home, named devvm-img-<key>. devvm makes base’s from Ubuntu’s cloud image with base.yaml, base’s size as --cpus, --memory and --disk, and --mount-none, and it gives limactl create the template on its standard input (-), from the binary, so no copy of base.yaml is on disk. With --from, it makes base’s from the converted disk instead, and boots its kernel and initrd directly (details). A layer’s image is a clone of its parent’s, also made with --mount-none, so a build mounts nothing from the host. A project VM is a clone of its image’s VM, which devvm makes while the image is stopped.

  • macOS: the clone’s disk is an APFS copy-on-write copy. It shares the image’s blocks until the VM writes them, so du overcounts it.
  • Linux: Lima’s disks are qcow2 files, and a clone would be a full copy. So a project VM’s disk is a qcow2 overlay of its image’s, readable only by you, which shares the image’s blocks and holds only the VM’s changes. An image’s disk is read-only once it’s built, and devvm can’t delete an image while VMs’ disks are overlays of it (image_in_use). devvm reads each VM disk’s backing file with qemu-img info -U, which shares the disk with the QEMU of a running VM, because that QEMU’s write lock refuses qemu-img info otherwise.

What devvm sets on a VM

devvm sets these in each VM’s Lima config:

  • Mounts: the project folder (read-write), agents’ folders (read-only), and the shared tools at /mnt/devvm-tools (read-only). Each folder but the tools is mounted at its host path. devvm mounts nothing else, and it leaves out the home folder that Lima’s templates mount. On macOS, where Lima runs VMs with vz, the project folder’s mount names the folder by the device and inode that devvm recorded when it made the VM, as location: /.vol/<device>/<inode> with mountPoint set to the folder’s path. macOS’s /.vol opens a folder by its device and inode, so Virtualization.framework shares the folder devvm made the VM for, wherever that folder is when the VM starts, and never follows a link put at its path (an existing VM). Virtualization.framework then serves the share by the path the folder had at the start, so a folder moved back while the VM runs answers “Operation not permitted” in the VM until its next start. QEMU’s 9p on Linux has nothing like /.vol, so there the mount is by the folder’s path, with the cache mode the VM’s state records as its 9p: cache: option: none for a new VM, and nothing for a VM whose mode nobody chose, which keeps Lima’s mmap (why). The read-only mounts keep Lima’s fscache, and a build VM’s writable output folder gets none. The start that changes a VM’s cache mode mounts its folder again once the VM runs, because the guest mounted it with the old options before cloud-init wrote the new ones into its /etc/fstab, and it then checks the mount: a folder left unmounted fails the start (why). A start that rewrites the mounts, for a folder that moved, another cache mode or other agents’ folders, keeps each mount’s settings that devvm doesn’t set, such as its other 9p and sshfs options, where they differ from Lima’s defaults, and leaves the defaults out for Lima to fill in.
  • ssh: agent forwarding on or off, and the host port. devvm chooses the port when it makes the VM and records it, so no other VM’s forwarded ports take it. The port changes only when another program on the host has it, on any address, while the VM is stopped, or when the VM lists it to forward.
  • Ports: none, because Lima’s own forwards are off and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead (below).
  • Size: CPUs, memory and disk.
  • Guest environment: Lima’s env:, which Lima writes to /etc/environment at every boot. On every tier it holds the VM’s proxy’s address and its settings, and Lima doesn’t pass the host’s proxy settings in. A confined VM reaches the proxy as Lima’s host address on macOS and as QEMU’s guestfwd address on Linux, and an open VM reaches it at Lima’s host address on both, which is this machine’s loopback as Lima’s network has it, with host.lima.internal added to its NO_PROXY. limactl edit sets the proxy’s URL with a stand-in for the password (devvm-proxy-password), and devvm then replaces the stand-in in the VM’s lima.yaml, which it rewrites with mode 600, so the password is in no process’s arguments. Its NO_PROXY and no_proxy name the VM alone, and never its links, which its HTTP clients reach through the proxy, so links never change it. A start runs limactl edit only when the environment differs from the one the VM has, because it compares them first. That edit gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot, as any edit does, and devvm forgets a VM’s host keys at every start and pins them again once it runs, so devvm’s ssh config, its own connections and your editors keep working.
  • Proxy settings and DNS: Lima’s propagateProxyEnv, which writes this machine’s proxy settings into the guest, is on only for a VM on Lima’s own network without devvm’s proxy, so they never reach a VM that goes through devvm’s proxy. A VM confined to its proxy has Lima’s host resolver off (hostResolver.enabled: false) and dns: ["127.0.0.1"], because its names resolve in the proxy (confinement). An open VM keeps Lima’s own resolver and DNS.

Lima changes only a stopped VM’s config, so a change you make while the VM runs applies at its next start. When devvm makes a VM, the clone gets its mounts, agent forwarding, ssh port, ports rules and environment, and devvm then edits the VM’s size where it differs from its image’s. Each start of a stopped VM compares the VM’s config, as limactl list shows it, with what the VM’s state asks for and with how the VM starts. That covers its size, its project folder’s path, which changes once the folder moved (a moved folder), on macOS the device and inode its mount names, and on Linux its cache mode where one was chosen, its agents’ folders, its agent forwarding, its ssh port, its environment, Lima’s proxy settings (propagateProxyEnv), its DNS (hostResolver and dns) and its ports rules. devvm then changes whatever differs in one limactl edit, and runs none when nothing does, because each edit gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot. Lima can’t shrink a disk, so a start that asks for a smaller disk than the VM has fails before it changes anything (disk_shrink).

devvm leaves Lima’s mountInotify off, so file watchers in the VM see only the changes made in the VM (file watchers). With it on, Lima’s hostagent watches the project folder on the host and, for each change there, changes the file’s times in the guest as root, which raises an inotify event for the guest’s watchers. The hostagent can’t tell the VM’s own writes from the host’s, so it does this to every file the VM writes too, and on macOS the guest then sees such a file as root’s for a moment. A command that writes a file and then changes its mode fails in that moment, and in a test on macOS, git init in the project folder failed 13 times in 30 with it on and never with it off. Lima also passes on no deletions, and it marks the setting as experimental.

Confinement

A VM on a confined tier, internet, allowlist or none, reaches nothing but its proxy on the host, which applies its tier’s rules, and even root in the VM can’t get around that. Direct connections, DNS, UDP and connections to the host’s own services fail at once, while forwarded ports, mounts and ssh keep working.

On each host, the VM’s traffic passes through one process that devvm confines:

flowchart TD
subgraph linux["Linux"]
vm2["the VM"] --> q["QEMU,<br>restrict=on"]
end
q -- "only to<br>192.168.5.4:3128" --> proxy["its proxy"]
subgraph mac["macOS"]
vm1["the VM"] --> ha["its Lima<br>hostagent,<br>sandboxed"]
end
ha -- "allowed" --> ok["its ssh port<br>its proxy<br>its Lima sockets<br>its SSH agent"]
ha -. "denied" .-> no["everything<br>else"]

On macOS, devvm starts the VM’s Lima process, its hostagent, under a macOS sandbox. That’s sandbox-exec with a Seatbelt profile, sandbox.sb in the VM’s run folder, ~/.local/share/devvm/vms/<hash>/run/.

  • The profile lets the process connect to the VM’s ssh port and its proxy on the host’s loopback, to the unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder (ssh’s control socket and the VM’s network), and to the ssh agent the VM forwards, which is yours or devvm’s own. It connects nowhere else, so other sockets on the host, such as Docker’s, stay out of the hostagent’s reach. The profile limits only the network, so a compromised hostagent can still write your files, and through them run code as you.
  • The profile lets the process listen only on the VM’s ssh port, over TCP, and on unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder, so it can’t open a port of the VM’s on the host even if Lima ignored its rules (ports).
  • Names resolve in the proxy, so Lima’s own DNS server for the VM is off, and the guest’s DNS points at 127.0.0.1, which only transparent mode answers, inside the VM, with no upstream. Without it, nothing listens there, and a lookup through the system’s resolver, as getent and curl make one, fails at once on macOS and on a Linux host alike. On a Linux host, where the VM lists only 127.0.0.1 as its DNS server, a few tools that resolve names their own way, such as workerd under wrangler dev, wait about 40 seconds for each lookup before they fail. The guest reaches the proxy at 192.168.5.2, which is the host as Lima’s network sees it.

On Linux, Lima starts every VM’s QEMU through a wrapper that devvm writes (~/.local/share/devvm/run/qemu/) and that runs devvm. It runs QEMU in a namespace that makes .git’s hooks and config read-only, for a VM whose .git protection is on. For a confined VM, the wrapper adds QEMU’s restrict=on to Lima’s network, so no traffic goes in or out but Lima’s own forwards. It also adds one address, 192.168.5.4:3128, which QEMU connects to the VM’s proxy. If Lima’s QEMU arguments aren’t the shape devvm expects, with one -netdev user,id=net0,… and no other network, the wrapper refuses to start QEMU (qemu_refused), so QEMU never runs unrestricted. DNS points at 127.0.0.1 in the guest, which only transparent mode answers, and without it lookups fail at once.

An open VM isn’t confined: on macOS its hostagent runs without a profile, and on Linux the wrapper runs QEMU with Lima’s network as Lima gives it, without restrict=on and without the guestfwd, as it does for a build with the internet. Its guest reaches its proxy at 192.168.5.2 and the proxy’s own port on both hosts, because Lima’s user-mode network, vz’s and QEMU’s alike, reaches the host’s loopback at that address. Its NO_PROXY adds host.lima.internal and 192.168.5.2, which the proxy on the host couldn’t resolve as the VM does, Lima’s DNS stays on, so names resolve in the VM, and propagateProxyEnv is off, so the guest gets no proxy settings of the host’s.

A process can’t leave its sandbox, so devvm records the hostagent it started (started in the VM’s run folder) and checks that the VM still runs on it (the self-check). A VM started another way, such as with limactl start, runs unconfined, and devvm ls shows it as unenforced. The VM’s proxy follows the hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid in the VM’s Lima folder) and exits with it. devvm writes the record only once limactl start returns, while the hostagent runs on its own from early in the start, so an interrupt during the start stops the VM (how long a proxy runs). Interrupted before the hostagent answers, the VM is one Lima reports as Broken, which limactl stop refuses, so devvm stops a broken VM with limactl stop --force. A hostagent that runs without its driver yet is still starting QEMU, which writes its pid file only once it runs, and that can take seconds on a slow host, such as one with nested virtualization. Stopped with --force then, the hostagent would go and the QEMU it started would run on without it, so devvm waits up to 30 seconds for the driver first and then stops the VM as Lima reports it. A VM whose QEMU still runs without its hostagent holds its disk, so no new QEMU can start on it, and a start stops such a VM with --force first.

Builds are also confined, because they run code devvm didn’t write. On macOS a build’s Lima process runs under a profile that reaches either the internet but not the host’s loopback, where other VMs’ proxies and dev servers listen, or nothing at all. Behind a company proxy, a build with the internet also reaches one port of the host’s loopback, its own proxy’s (a company proxy). On Linux only a build with no network is confined. QEMU can’t keep the internet while dropping the host’s loopback, so other builds reach services on the host’s localhost. Builds forward no ports. A build with the internet reaches your LAN on both hosts, this machine’s own address on it included, because the macOS profile keeps only the loopback from it.

sandbox-exec is deprecated. If macOS drops it, devvm needs another way to confine the hostagent, and until then the self-check catches a VM that runs unconfined.

Ports

devvm’s forwarder forwards a Lima VM’s ports by the rules that Port forwarding sets out. On Lima this is an emulation, and it’s reviewed (design). devvm doesn’t use Lima’s own forwards because they listen with SO_REUSEADDR, and on macOS such a forward takes 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program on the host has *:PORT, along with that program’s localhost connections.

So Lima forwards nothing. Each VM’s portForwards are rules that ignore every guest port, TCP and UDP, on 127.0.0.1 (which also covers ::1), 0.0.0.0 and ::. Lima’s own ssh is its VM driver’s forward, not a rule, so it keeps working. devvm sets the rules when it makes the VM, and a start sets them again only where they differ, because any change gives the VM new ssh host keys at its next boot. On macOS, a confined VM doesn’t rely on the rules alone, because its sandbox refuses the Lima process every port but its ssh port (confinement).

Which ports a VM forwards is in the VM’s state, which devvm’s forwarder reads, so devvm ports changes the state and never the VM’s Lima config, and the backend never hears of them. Its process and files lists the forwarder’s files and its log.

The forwarder isn’t Lima’s, and it runs only for project VMs. What Lima gives it is how to reach a running VM: Lima’s ssh port on this machine’s loopback, Lima’s user, and Lima’s key (_config/user in devvm’s Lima home), which every VM there authorizes. The forwarder connects there with the host keys devvm pinned for the VM’s current start, which the VM’s ssh config checks too. Its lifeline is the VM’s hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid), so it ends when the hostagent does, and devvm rm deletes its files.

item.title: Coding agents
item.description:
This page explains how devvm gives the coding agents in a VM their settings, logins and history, and what it checks on the way, for the tasks that Coding agents shows. How the proxy holds the agents’ secrets is in agents’ logins and settings.

The guide in every VM

Each launch installs the guide again whenever it differs from devvm’s, and it belongs to root and is read-only, so nothing that the VM’s user runs without sudo can change what the agents read, and a change made with sudo lasts only until the next launch.

Pasting

How devvm paste reads the clipboard, names a copied file, refuses links and finds Linux’s clipboard programs is in the design note on pasting images.

Each agent’s variables

Every VM sets OPENCODE_DISABLE_AUTOUPDATE=1, as it sets DISABLE_AUTOUPDATER=1 for Claude Code, because the agents are read-only shared tools that can’t update themselves, and devvm keeps their versions. For the same reason every VM sets PI_SKIP_VERSION_CHECK=1, so pi doesn’t ask you to run pi update, and PI_TELEMETRY=0, which turns off pi’s report of its install and the attribution headers it adds to some providers’ requests. Claude Code’s telemetry and error reports are off with DISABLE_TELEMETRY=1 and DISABLE_ERROR_REPORTING=1. devvm writes every agent’s variables into each VM at every launch, whichever agents the VM has, and every shell in the VM gets them, login or not, so an agent that an editor’s terminal or ssh runs gets them too. pi would download fd and rg into ~/.pi/agent/bin whenever they’re missing, so base has both, from Ubuntu’s or the container image’s own packages, and pi finds Ubuntu’s and Debian’s fd by its name there, fdfind.

Importing

The import copies only the paths in the store’s table, from ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.config/opencode, ~/.local/share/opencode and ~/.pi/agent, so it never copies your history, such as ~/.claude/projects, ~/.codex’s sessions or ~/.pi/agent/sessions, and never ~/.claude/.credentials.json. Claude Code’s plugin records name the plugins’ folders by their paths, so the store’s copies of the JSON files in ~/.claude/plugins name the plugins’ folders in the store, where the VMs mount them.

A replacement writes each file again and takes out what your home folder no longer has, but it keeps the store’s folders, so a running VM’s mounts still show them. Where the store has a folder and the home folder now has a file, or the other way round, as when a link that led to a folder now leads to a file, the import replaces it.

opencode 2 keeps its logins in its own database rather than in ~/.local/share/opencode/auth.json, so when this machine’s opencode is version 2 or later, devvm reads its logins with opencode auth export and saves them in the store in the format of auth.json, the file that devvm copies for opencode 1. When opencode auth export fails, the import fails too, and the store keeps the login it had.

Links out of an agent’s folder

The import reads each agent’s folder through that folder as an os.Root, so no link inside it leads out of it. A link that leads out is resolved, every link on the way, and only then followed, as links out of an agent’s folder says, and the design note explains why:

  • How it resolves. devvm resolves a link one name at a time, as the system does, and keeps where each link on the way is, so it sees a link that a VM put in its project folder even in the middle of a chain. It compares a target with the refused places and the VMs’ folders by name and by identity, so another spelling of a folder, such as ~/.SSH on a Mac, where case doesn’t count, is still that folder.
  • Where it reads. devvm opens the folder it reads the link’s target through, a follow-links folder, the linked folder or the linked file’s own folder, one folder at a time from /, each opened from its parent and never through a link, so a link that a VM swaps into that path fails the import rather than lead elsewhere. It lists what the link leads to through that folder as a root, and reads each file without blocking, refusing a FIFO, a device or a file that changed into a link as it opened it.
  • What it lists. A linked folder’s folders and files are listed under the link’s own path, and a link inside it is listed as a file when the root resolves it to a regular file. Anything else is left out with a warning.
  • The bounds. It counts every file and folder it lists, and the size of every file, across all the links of one import, and leaves out a link that would pass 20,000 entries, 128 MiB or a file of 16 MiB, the bounds of saving a VM’s settings. A file that grows past them between the listing and the read fails the import.
  • A VM’s folder. It reads the state of every VM devvm has, and warns once for each link and VM when the link’s target is in that VM’s project folder or holds it, or when a link inside a linked folder resolves into it.

Saving a VM’s settings

The save reads only the settings in the store’s table from the VM’s home, and never the logins, so it never reads your history, ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, opencode’s auth.json or pi’s. From the VM’s ~/.claude.json it keeps only the settings, account state and MCP servers, as the import does, and the VM leaves out its per-project entries before it sends anything. devvm puts that part in the store’s logins folder, where the import keeps it too. A folder that the store already has is mounted read-only in the VM, so the agent there can’t change it, and the save leaves it as it is. A folder that the store doesn’t have yet is the VM’s own until you save it, and once the VM next starts with the store’s new folder mounted, its setup links that folder in place of its own (mounts).

devvm treats everything the VM sends as untrusted, because the agent in the VM could have changed any of it. It reads at most 128 MiB from the VM, in at most 20,000 files, folders and links, none of the files larger than 16 MiB, and when the VM sends more, or sends a path outside the agents’ settings or a name with a character that a terminal wouldn’t show, devvm saves nothing. Each file it saves is yours alone (mode 600), or mode 700 when it was executable in the VM, so it never keeps a set-user-ID or set-group-ID bit. A link in a settings folder that leads to a file in the same folder becomes a copy of that file. devvm leaves out any other link, any other kind of file, such as a socket, and a settings file that it can’t parse whole, such as a settings.json that isn’t JSON, and it warns you about each. When it leaves out a file in a folder, the store keeps its own copy of that file. A settings file that the VM doesn’t have stays in the store. A folder that the VM sends replaces the store’s folder whole, so devvm writes each of its files again and takes out the files that the VM’s folder doesn’t have, but it keeps the store’s folder itself, so a running VM’s mounts still show it.

The VM’s copies of the settings files and of ~/.claude.json hold placeholders, such as devvm-redacted, where the store has your secrets. devvm puts the store’s secret back in place of each placeholder, as long as the VM’s copy had that placeholder in that place and nothing around it changed, such as the URL of the MCP server that a header is for. When something around a placeholder changed, devvm leaves the whole file out and warns you, so a VM can’t send a secret it never saw to another host, and you can make that change in the store’s file yourself. devvm also leaves out any other file that holds a placeholder, such as a skill. No VM gets opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env, so devvm leaves out the VM’s own file of that name and keeps the store’s.

Mounts

Absolute paths in the mounted folders, such as Claude Code’s plugin paths, still work, because each is mounted at the same path as in the store on this machine. The VM follows a symlink in these folders among its own files, so a link to a file outside the folder, by a relative or an absolute path, doesn’t reach that file on this machine, on macOS’s virtiofs mounts and on Linux’s 9p mounts alike. devvm doesn’t mount a folder whose path has a comma, on any backend, and it warns you. Lima can’t mount such a path (Lima’s limits).

Copies

devvm merges the settings and MCP servers from the store’s .claude.json into the VM’s own ~/.claude.json, so servers added in the VM stay (MCP servers). Your API key, your answers about API keys and your per-project entries never reach the VM. devvm also replaces the secrets in the agents’ settings files with devvm-redacted, and names what it replaced. Those are the values under keys that look like secrets, every env value and header, and the secrets in URLs and in arguments. In other text, such as a hook’s command, devvm replaces the secrets in its URLs, the keys that start like a known key, such as sk- or ghp_, and the credential after Bearer or Basic, and keeps the words around them (keys in settings files). pi’s settings files that can hold a key are settings.json, models.json and mcp.json, so a provider’s apiKey in models.json reaches the VM as devvm-redacted, and pi’s keybindings.json and Markdown files reach it as they are. From the env of Claude Code’s settings.json, the VM gets only Claude Code’s own settings, such as ANTHROPIC_MODEL, the CLAUDE_CODE_*, DISABLE_* and MAX_* variables and those ending in _TIMEOUT_MS, but none whose name marks it as a credential, such as ANTHROPIC_AUTH_TOKEN. It also gets the values that only name where a secret is, base URLs without their passwords, true, false and short numbers. Every other env value, and every env value of an MCP server, becomes devvm-redacted. When devvm can’t parse a settings file to take its secrets out, the VM doesn’t get a copy of it, and neither does it get opencode’s files in ~/.config/opencode that are neither settings nor Markdown, such as a .env. devvm names each file it doesn’t copy, and when it can’t make the copy of a login, it says why.

Claude Code’s login

devvm agent login claude runs Claude Code’s own login in the VM, and the VM’s proxy saves the login as it reaches Claude’s token endpoint, and Claude Code in the VM gets only placeholders. devvm then sets the VM up again, so it uses the login at once, and every other VM with Claude Code gets it from its next launch.

A VM gets either ~/.claude/.credentials.json or CLAUDE_CODE_OAUTH_TOKEN from devvm, never both, because Claude Code would use the token in its environment over the login in its file. A VM that started with the login devvm replaced keeps working, because its proxy puts the login devvm keeps now in place of either placeholder. The VM gets placeholders whatever its network tier.

Codex’s and opencode’s logins

The proxy reads the real API keys and logins from the login files in devvm’s store as it needs them and refreshes ChatGPT logins there. The proxy puts in opencode’s API keys for the providers that API keys the proxy puts in lists, and its OpenAI and GitHub Copilot logins. The VM’s entry for such an API key holds only its type and the placeholder, so the entry’s other fields, such as its metadata, stay on this machine.

The VM’s copy of Codex’s auth.json holds only what Codex needs for its API key and its ChatGPT login: the placeholders, how it logs in, when it last refreshed, and the IDs of the account and the login. devvm keeps every other field on this machine, because the VM’s proxy can’t put it in, and it names those fields at every launch. That includes Codex’s other ways to log in, such as a personal access token or an Amazon Bedrock key, so Codex in a VM can’t use them. devvm treats Claude Code’s account state in ~/.claude.json the same way, so the VM gets only the account fields that Claude Code writes there today, and devvm names any other field at every launch.

devvm keeps every other entry of opencode’s auth.json on this machine too, because devvm doesn’t know which hosts it’s for, so the VM gets that entry without its key or its tokens, and devvm warns you about each at every launch. That’s an API key for any other provider, such as Azure’s or a local model server’s, a well-known login, which an organization’s own opencode config sets up, and any other OAuth login, such as Copilot Enterprise’s. The VM keeps only the fields of a withheld entry that name the account or how it logs in, such as its type, its enterpriseUrl and its expiry, so opencode in the VM doesn’t use that provider.

Logging in

When you approve a browser login, the browser comes back to localhost:1455, where the agent’s own server in the VM waits, so devvm forwards this machine’s localhost:1455, and localhost:1457, which Codex uses when 1455 is taken in the VM, to the same ports in the VM. The forward lasts only while the login runs, and it ends when the login ends, fails or you press Ctrl+C, which ends the agent’s login in the VM too.

Codex in a VM keeps its login in ~/.codex/auth.json, never in a keyring, because devvm sets cli_auth_credentials_store = "file" in the VM’s ~/.codex/config.toml on every launch.

With --api-key, devvm gives the running VM its copy of the login, with a placeholder in place of the key, and the VM’s proxy puts the key in at once. opencode keeps its logins in its own database in the VM, and it reads its auth.json only when it first makes that database, so when opencode has already run in the VM, devvm also gives it the key’s placeholder with opencode auth import. devvm reads at most 1 MiB of what that import prints in the VM, and when it prints more, devvm stops it and fails, so running devvm in the VM’s folder tries again. Every other VM with opencode gets the key’s placeholder at its next launch, the same way, and any credentials that you added to opencode in a VM yourself stay in its database.

Logins made in a VM

When Codex or opencode in a VM logs in to OpenAI, whether devvm agent login runs it or you run it yourself, the VM’s proxy saves the login in devvm’s store, in the agent’s own auth.json, and the agent in the VM gets only placeholders, so on every tier but open the VM never holds the login’s tokens. The VM you logged in from uses the login at once, and every VM with that agent gets it from its next launch. opencode reads its auth.json only when it first makes its database, so in a VM where opencode has already run, devvm adds the store’s logins to opencode’s database at each launch when they changed since the VM last got them, and makes them the ones opencode uses. Credentials that you added to opencode in the VM yourself stay in its database, labeled with your names rather than devvm, and opencode auth switch changes back to one of them. A login that shows a code to type into a browser on any machine works in a VM as it is, such as codex login --device-auth and opencode’s Codex device code login. opencode’s Sign in with ChatGPT doesn’t work in a VM, because it gets its tokens from another endpoint, whose replies the VM’s proxy refuses so that they never reach the VM, so choose one of opencode’s Codex logins instead, as devvm agent login opencode does. A new login replaces the one in the store, together with Codex’s API key, so every VM with the agent uses the account you logged in to last. A VM saves a login only for an agent that it has, so a VM without Codex can’t replace the store’s Codex login, and a VM without opencode can’t replace opencode’s. When a VM sends a login for an agent it doesn’t have, such as one that a program installed in the VM itself, its proxy refuses the login, devvm saves nothing, and the proxy’s own log says so. In a VM with both Codex and opencode, devvm tells their logins apart by the program that sends them. devvm network log shows a login line for each login it saved. On the open tier, a program that goes around the VM’s proxy gets the login’s tokens itself, and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM). Claude Code’s logins in a VM are saved in the same way (Claude Code login).

pi’s logins

devvm agent login pi --api-key --provider PROVIDER saves the key in the store’s ~/.local/share/devvm/logins/pi/.pi/agent/auth.json, in pi’s own format, beside pi’s other providers, as opencode’s --api-key does (logging in with devvm agent login). The VM’s ~/.pi/agent/auth.json holds a placeholder in place of each of those keys, and the VM’s proxy puts the key into pi’s requests to that provider’s hosts, on every network tier, and allows those hosts, as the table in API keys the proxy puts in describes. The VM’s entry for such a provider holds only its type and the placeholder, so it gets none of the entry’s other fields, such as its env, whose values pi uses before the environment’s, and the store keeps them on this machine.

devvm keeps every other entry of pi’s auth.json on this machine too, and the VM gets that entry without its key, its env or its tokens, and devvm warns you about each. That’s an API key for any other provider, such as a local model server’s, a key that’s a command for pi to run, such as !security find-generic-password, and a key that pi fills in from a variable, such as $KEY or ${KEY}, even for a provider whose key the proxy puts in, because devvm can’t tell what pi would send. The VM keeps only the fields of a withheld entry that name the account or how it logs in, such as its type, its accountId and its expiry.

pi’s Claude and ChatGPT logins use the same token endpoints as Claude Code’s, Codex’s and opencode’s logins, whose replies the VM’s proxy captures for those agents, and devvm never keeps such a login as pi’s. In a VM that also has the matching agent, Claude Code for a Claude login and Codex or opencode for a ChatGPT login, the proxy saves pi’s login as that agent’s own, in place of the one devvm keeps for every VM with that agent. In a VM with none of them, the proxy refuses pi’s login and devvm saves nothing (logins made in a VM).

Cursor’s CLI

The VM’s proxy puts the real login only into the requests for the methods that devvm found the CLI calling in its package, on Cursor’s API, its agent’s hosts and its codebase indexing, and into no other. It refuses every other request below /auth/ on those hosts, the methods that make or show a key, a token, a secret or a sign-in, the methods that change your account, and any path it can’t read as Cursor’s hosts do. Those are the real control. As a defence in depth, the proxy also reads every reply from those hosts as it passes, its headers and the agent’s streams included, and cuts one off where a token starts. devvm checked this against one release of the CLI, by reading its code, and against Cursor’s own answers to a login that isn’t there, so a method that Cursor adds that hands out a token in a shape devvm doesn’t know would reach the VM. Such a token would work without the proxy, so if you suspect that one reached a VM, log in again with devvm agent login cursor (logins made in a VM). Neither does devvm guard Cursor’s hosts that the CLI doesn’t use: if one of them also answered /auth/poll, a VM could finish a login there and keep its tokens, though none is known to.

Your Cursor agents on every machine and in the cloud share Cursor’s agent store, your cloud agents follow the skills in it, and your team shares a store of its own, so a VM that could write there could leave instructions for them. So no VM gets the store (why).

API keys

The proxy puts in opencode’s and pi’s API keys for the providers that API keys the proxy puts in lists, in the headers it names. OpenRouter’s key goes in either of its two headers, because pi sends it in x-api-key for OpenRouter’s Anthropic models, as Anthropic’s own API takes a key, and in Authorization for every other model. The proxy swaps the placeholder only when the header holds the placeholder and nothing else, or for Authorization, Bearer, one space and the placeholder, which is how opencode and pi send each of these keys. A header that holds anything else beside the placeholder, or a second header of the same name, keeps the placeholder, so code in the VM can’t surround your key with text of its own, which a provider that quotes part of a key it refuses could show back to it.

The placeholder for an OpenAI key starts with sk-, as an OpenAI API key does, because pi takes an OpenAI key that starts any other way for a Sign in with ChatGPT login and then leaves settings such as the longest reply it wants out of its requests.

The placeholder keeps a key out of the VM only from the launch that first gives the VM the placeholder. A VM that was given one of these keys as it was before then, such as through [pass-keys] when the proxy didn’t put that provider’s key in, may still hold copies of it. They can be in opencode’s database, its write-ahead log and its freed pages, in the disk’s free space and anywhere that the VM’s own code copied the key. While opencode in the VM fails to import the placeholder, devvm’s record of opencode’s last import, ~/.local/state/devvm/opencode-import.json, holds the key too.

With some of these keys, code in the VM can make a credential of its own that works without the proxy. Google Gemini’s key gets an ephemeral token for Gemini’s Live API, which lasts up to about 20 hours and allows as many uses as the VM asks for. xAI’s key gets a realtime client secret that lasts as long as the VM chooses, and OpenAI’s key gets one that lasts up to 2 hours. opencode’s experimental voice mode asks for these itself, so the proxy allows those requests (attack vectors). Some of these providers’ own tools also fetch the URLs that a request names, such as Google Gemini’s URL context and Search grounding, xAI’s live search, Groq’s compound models and Mistral’s agents with web search, so code in the VM can reach hosts that the allowlist doesn’t have through them, as it can through Anthropic’s and OpenAI’s.

History exports

The agents’ logins aren’t in the export, which leaves out ~/.claude/.credentials.json, ~/.codex/auth.json, and opencode’s auth.json, account.json, mcp-auth.json and bin, and holds nothing of ~/.pi/agent but its sessions, so pi’s auth.json stays out too. opencode keeps its sessions and its logins together in one database, ~/.local/share/opencode/opencode.db, so the export holds a copy of that database without its logins. The VM makes the copy with sqlite3, which every base image has, and the copy has no logins, API keys or opencode account in any part of the file, not even a key you typed into opencode in the VM, while the VM’s own database keeps them (how). The export never holds the database’s -wal, -shm or -journal files, which can hold logins that opencode saved last. When the VM has no sqlite3, such as a VM made from an image built without it, the export leaves the database out, so opencode’s sessions aren’t in it, and the run log says so. devvm starts a stopped VM for the export as a launch does, so it locks the folder’s .git again and checks the VM’s confinement first, and the VM stays running. devvm writes the file only once the export is complete, so a failed export leaves no file and leaves an existing FILE as it was. An export holds at most 2 GiB, because a VM could otherwise write until this machine’s disk is full. When the VM sends more, devvm stops the export and keeps nothing of it, so devvm history export fails, while devvm rm and the commands that make a VM again warn that they kept no export and go on without one. Only you can read the file, and devvm makes the exports folder yours alone each time it writes one there, whatever its mode was before. When FILE is in a folder of your own, that folder keeps its mode. If the export fails, devvm rm keeps the VM, and devvm rm --no-export deletes it without exporting. devvm rm VM, for a VM whose folder is gone, exports in the same way, but only from a running VM or a --clone VM, because starting any other would make its folder again (a VM whose folder is gone).

Importing history

The import works on every VM, whether its base is Ubuntu’s image or a Debian-, Ubuntu- or Alpine-based container image (starting from a container image), because it unpacks the export with GNU tar, which Debian and Ubuntu always have and which devvm installs in every base made --from alpine.

An export holds what a VM wrote, so devvm treats it as untrusted. Its transcripts can hold what the old VM’s agents read, and a VM on a less strict tier reaches more, such as your local network on the open tier. So when the export comes from a VM on a less strict tier than the VM you import it into, going from open to internet, allowlist and none, devvm warns you before it imports. devvm knows an export’s tier only from the .folder file beside it in ~/.local/share/devvm/exports, so it warns about an export with no tier recorded, or any FILE elsewhere, such as in the project folder that a VM can write, as if it came from an open VM. devvm never unpacks an export on this machine. It streams the file into the VM as it is, and the VM’s own tar unpacks it there as the VM’s user, so it can only write what that user can write. Before unpacking anything, the VM lists the paths in the export, and when one of them is outside ~/.claude, ~/.claude.json, ~/.codex, ~/.local/share/opencode, ~/.local/state/opencode, ~/.pi/agent/sessions and ~/.cursor/chats, starts with / or has a .. part, devvm imports nothing and says so. It leaves out of that check, and never unpacks, the AppleDouble files whose names start with ._, which macOS’s tar puts beside each file that has extended attributes, so an export you packed yourself on a Mac imports. The import keeps no owner or mode from the export, so the VM user’s umask applies and no file is set-user-ID. It also takes out every symbolic link that points outside the folder it’s in, which is any link to an absolute path or one with a .. part, so an agent writing to a session file can’t follow a link out of its history. An export that devvm didn’t write, such as a .tar.gz you made yourself, can hold opencode’s database with its logins, so the import takes out the database’s -wal, -shm and -journal files and puts in a copy of the database without its logins, as the export makes it, or leaves the database out when the VM has no sqlite3. opencode in the new VM then reads the logins that devvm gave the VM, as it does when it first makes its database. When the VM already has an opencode database, it keeps its own, and opencode’s sessions from the export aren’t imported.

item.title: Design notes
item.description:
For contributors: why devvm is built the way it is, what was tried and dropped, and what’s still open. How each part works is on its own page, and Contributing has the repo’s layout and rules.

Emulated features

When devvm builds a backend feature from other parts of the backend, the feature is emulated, and it gets a note here before its review. The note says what the feature is built from, the guarantee it keeps, what could break it, and which end-to-end checks prove it. The threat check comes next, and only then is the feature marked reviewed. Every feature Lima has is native except its ports, which devvm’s forwarder emulates (below).

ssh into VMs

ssh for editors is native on Lima, so it isn’t an emulation, but its sessions keep a guarantee of devvm’s own: ssh and editors reach a VM by name through the entries devvm writes (security model), and a session gives the VM no way out it doesn’t already have, on a confined tier nothing past its proxy, whatever the VM runs as sshd.

What keeps a session from carrying the VM out. An ssh session can carry the VM’s traffic only through channels the host’s ssh asks for: remote forwards (-R, RemoteForward, a remote SOCKS forward), X11, a tunnel and the agent; OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel the server opens unasked. Root in the VM runs whatever sshd it likes, so the guarantee is the host’s ssh’s: devvm’s entry (first in ~/.ssh/config, so its options win over a Host *) sets ForwardX11 no, ForwardX11Trusted no, Tunnel no, PermitRemoteOpen none (so devvm needs OpenSSH 8.7 or newer; no IgnoreUnknown for older ones, as its first value wins and would replace a user’s Host * one, such as macOS’s for UseKeychain), ForwardAgent as the agent choice the VM’s current start was made with says, AddKeysToAgent no (no key of the host’s lands in an agent the session forwards), ProxyJump none and ProxyCommand none (no hop through something else), UpdateHostKeys no (the VM can’t add host keys; devvm reads them itself) and HashKnownHosts no. A RemoteForward can’t be turned off without refusing ssh -R on the command line too, so it isn’t (Not covered). VS Code’s Remote-SSH uses local and dynamic forwards (-L, -D) and is unaffected. Then sshd’s own settings, a defence for an honest VM (assets/layers/base.sh, /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/00-devvm.conf, first so it wins; Lima’s own forwards are local; it applies only where the image’s sshd_config includes sshd_config.d, as Ubuntu’s and Debian’s do, so for some --from images not at all, which only an honest VM’s defence loses):

  • Local forwarding (-L, -D, -W) is allowed: the VM itself connects, from its own network, which its tier confines like any other connection of the VM’s (checked). VS Code’s Remote-SSH reaches its server this way.
  • Remote forwards bind only 127.77.0.0/16, the range devvm keeps for links between VMs, and remote socket forwards are refused. A remote forward makes the host connect on the VM’s behalf, so one the host’s ssh asked for by mistake could reach anything the host reaches, its loopback services and sockets (docker.sock, agents) included, around the VM’s confinement. GatewayPorts clientspecified binds the address a request names, and PermitListen 127.77.*:* matches that address as text, so a request for localhost (ssh’s default), 127.0.0.1, 0.0.0.0 or ::1 is refused. Only devvm on the host asks for a forward in that range, always by number. X11 and tunnels are refused too.
  • Agent forwarding is allowed: the entry decides it from the SSH agent choice the VM’s current start was made with (ForwardAgent, devvm’s own agent too); refusing it would break devvm ssh-agent on in editors.

These settings guard against the host’s ssh asking for a forward that devvm’s entry doesn’t pin (a RemoteForward under Host *, ssh -R), and only while root in the VM leaves sshd as it is. They’re a safeguard for an honest VM, and the boundary is the host’s ssh, which accepts a channel only for a forward it asked for.

What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client refusing unrequested channels, and devvm’s Include line first in ~/.ssh/config, so its entries’ options win.

What could break it: host ssh settings that come before devvm’s entries.

Not covered:

  • A remote forward you ask for (ssh -R, a RemoteForward of yours): remote forwards you add lists what it leaves open.
  • Sessions see the proxy’s password, as devvm’s own shells do, and VS Code relays what VS Code describes.

Ports on Lima

The guarantee: when a VM forwards every port, each TCP port from 1024 up that a server in it listens on, on its loopback or on all its addresses, is forwarded to the same port on the host’s loopback, and only to its loopback. When a VM lists its ports, only those are forwarded, however many it lists, by the same rules. The forwarder never takes a port that a program on the host has on any address when the forward is made, or a port devvm records for another VM. Forwarding gives the VM no way out that it doesn’t already have, because every connection starts on the host. Lima’s own forwards listen with SO_REUSEADDR, so on macOS, whenever a server in the VM starts, Lima takes 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program on the host has *:PORT, and that program’s loopback connections go with it. That’s why Lima forwards nothing and devvm’s forwarder forwards the VM’s ports instead. On macOS, a confined VM doesn’t depend on Lima for that, because its hostagent’s sandbox refuses it every port but its ssh port, so Lima can’t forward a port of the VM’s even if it ignored its rules. The emulation is reviewed, with the threat check’s findings fixed or listed below, which is why the host key read is capped, reports are paced and the log is limited, and the end-to-end checks prove the rest.

What it’s built from:

  • Lima’s forwards off. Each VM’s portForwards holds three ignore rules, each for every guest port and protocol (any, which is TCP and UDP). They’re on 127.0.0.1, which Lima also matches for ::1, on 0.0.0.0 and on ::, which together match servers on all addresses. They come ahead of Lima’s own last rule, which forwards everything. CreateVM sets them with limactl clone --set. Start sets them only where limactl list shows other rules, because an edit gives the VM new host keys at its next boot. Lima’s ssh is its VM driver’s forward (ssh.localPort), not a rule, so the ignore rules leave it alone, and they cover the guest’s own ssh port like any other.
  • The sandbox’s binds (macOS, confined tiers). The hostagent of a confined VM runs under a Seatbelt profile (confinement) that denies every network bind but two kinds. It may bind the VM’s ssh port over TCP, which devvm chooses and records in the VM’s state (the ports section’s host.ssh), and unix sockets in the VM’s Lima folder, which hold the hostagent’s own socket (ha.sock), the VM’s network (default_ep.sock, default_fd.sock) and ssh’s control socket. Seatbelt matches a bind by its port alone, on any address, even when the rule names localhost, and it can’t allow an ephemeral bind (port 0) without allowing every port. It matches a unix socket by its path with links resolved, so a link in the Lima folder doesn’t let the hostagent bind a socket elsewhere. Lima’s host resolver binds two ephemeral ports for its DNS server, so a confined VM starts with the resolver off and 127.0.0.1 as its DNS server, as on Linux, where nothing listens and lookups fail at once. The hostagent reaches the guest agent over vsock, which needs no bind. This list comes from starting a VM under a profile that reported every bind, then under one that denied the rest: Lima logs a forward it’s refused (failed to listen) and carries on, while a refused resolver ends the start.
  • Which ports. Which ports each VM forwards, all, none or a list, is in its state (ports.forward), and the backend never hears of them: neither Start’s Want nor any other call of the backend’s has them. vmssh.Forwards.Start, the one owner of the forwarder, reads them from the VM’s state each time it starts one, after a start of the VM and when devvm ports changes a running VM’s ports, without editing Lima’s config. A stopped VM’s change is its state’s alone, because its next start reads it. When the VM lists ports, the forwarder forwards those less the ports a program on the host has, which the owner leaves out with a ports_taken warning. When none is left, no forwarder runs.
  • A forwarder per VM, on the host. The forwarder is vmssh.Forwarder, which isn’t a backend’s. Its owner, vmssh.Forwards, runs it detached as devvm _ports, one per VM, for project VMs alone, because only a project VM’s start goes through it, and builds’ starts don’t. The owner starts it once the backend’s Start returns, and again on a running VM when its ports change, each after stopping any forwarder the VM had, which ends the connections open through it. devvm finds that one by its pid file, which it checks against the process’s arguments, as it does for the proxy. It sends that forwarder SIGTERM and kills it if it hasn’t ended within 2 s, so its ports are free before devvm asks which listed ports a host program has. devvm holds a lock of the VM’s own (ports.lock, beside its pid file ports.pid in the VM’s run folder) from stopping the old forwarder until the new one has started, so two devvm runs at once, such as a start and devvm ports, leave one forwarder, the one its pid file names. The owner waits up to 10 s for the forwarder to say it forwards while it runs. The forwarder says so in a status file of its own beside its pid file (ports.status), which holds its pid and which devvm removes before each start. If it doesn’t, devvm warns with ports_forward_failed, naming its log, and leaves it to keep trying while the VM runs on.
  • Reaching the VM. The forwarder makes one ssh connection, a master (ssh -F none -M -S <socket>), to the VM’s sshd on Lima’s ssh port on the host’s loopback. Lima’s SSH gives the port with the user and the key, the first IdentityFile of Lima’s ssh config, and devvm refuses that target unless the config names 127.0.0.1 (vmssh.FromTarget, the check links and the ssh config use too). It logs in as Lima’s user with Lima’s key alone (IdentitiesOnly, IdentityAgent=none), _config/user in devvm’s Lima home, which every VM there authorizes, and never with the user’s agent. The master reads none of the user’s configuration and forwards nothing either way, with ClearAllForwardings, PermitRemoteOpen none, ProxyCommand none, and no agent, X11 or tunnel. The VM’s sshd allows local forwarding, and remote forwards only to 127.77.0.0/16 for links (base.sh), and -W is local forwarding. Its control socket is in ~/.local/share/devvm/run (mode 700) and is named by a hash of the VM’s name, because a socket’s path has fewer than 104 characters. When the connection is lost, the forwarder closes its forwards and makes the connection again every 2 s while the lifeline holds.
  • What listens. The master’s session runs ports.sh (assets/guest/ports.sh) as the VM’s user (sh -s). It prints the local addresses of the VM’s listening TCP sockets, which are the state 0A lines of /proc/net/tcp and tcp6, whenever they change and every 10 s regardless, so it ends soon after the connection does. The forwarder treats the report as untrusted. A line over 128 bytes or a report over 4096 lines ends the connection, and anything that isn’t a hex address and port is skipped. Reports are applied at least 500 ms apart, and one that comes sooner waits, holding up the VM’s ssh channel with it, so the VM can’t make the forwarder bind, dial and read devvm’s state at its own pace. The VM can make the forwarder write to its log, with ports coming and going and with the session’s stderr, so the log takes 200 writes at once and then one every 10 s. Each write is at most 512 bytes, without control characters but newlines and tabs, C1 included, and a start empties the log once it’s over 1 MiB. A forwarded port’s connections go to 127.0.0.1 for a server on all IPv4 addresses or on that address, and to ::1 for a server on all IPv6 addresses or on that address. A server on another 127.x address alone gets its connections there. Servers on other addresses alone aren’t forwarded.
  • How many. With every port, the forwarder takes ports from 1024 up, because the ports below are the host’s system services. With listed ports, it takes those alone (-only), a listed port below 1024 included, because the user asked for it, and a bind the host refuses is logged. Either way the forwarder takes at most 256 ports at once. It reads the reserved ports (below) again with each report, and while it can’t read them, it takes no new port and keeps those it has. A port it has that has since become reserved, such as one another VM’s start has chosen, is given up at that report, though the VM still listens on it. A port the forwarder couldn’t take is tried again only once the VM’s server on it goes and comes back.
  • Listening. The forwarder listens on 127.0.0.1 and ::1, or on IPv4 alone on a host without IPv6. It binds without SO_REUSEADDR (platform.ListenExclusive). With that option, which Go and Lima set, macOS lets a socket take 127.0.0.1:PORT while a program has *:PORT, and that program’s loopback connections go with it. Without the option, the bind is refused when another program has the port on any address. This was checked on macOS for a program on 0.0.0.0, on :: (IPv4 and IPv6 at once, as Node’s and Go’s servers listen), on IPv6 alone and on 127.0.0.1, each with and without SO_REUSEADDR of its own. A port held only by ended connections (TIME_WAIT, with nothing answering on it) is taken as usual, so a server that restarts gets its forward back. When a bind is refused, the forwarder dials the port and takes it only if the dial is refused. A full backlog times out, which counts as taken. A port the forwarder took on 127.0.0.1 but finds in use on ::1 is given up, so localhost never reaches two programs. On Linux, SO_REUSEADDR stays on. Linux refuses that bind with the option too while another socket listens on the port, and without it, the forwarder’s own ended connections (TIME_WAIT) would keep anyone from listening on the port for a minute, its next forwarder included.
  • Each connection. Each forwarded connection is a channel of the master’s (ssh -S <socket> -W HOST:PORT), with one process per connection and at most 256 at once. The VM’s sshd opens it to the VM’s own loopback from inside the VM. The channel’s ssh has the master’s options. If the master is gone, ssh connects on its own, and it then reaches the VM’s sshd the same way, never the host’s.
  • Reserved ports. The forwarder never takes the VM’s own Lima ssh port, which Lima’s SSH names, or its proxy port, which its state records, and the owner passes both as -reserve. It also never takes the ssh, proxy and desktop ports devvm chooses and records in any VM’s state, or other VMs’ listed ports (ports.Used). Every Lima VM’s ssh port is one of those, whatever its tier: devvm chooses it when it makes the VM, sets it with limactl clone --set .ssh.localPort, and records it in the VM’s ports section before the clone (ports.Allocator.SSH). One allocator, ports.Allocator, chooses every host port devvm chooses, the ssh, proxy and desktop ports, and records it while it holds the VM’s lock and then the claims lock (run/claims.lock, state.VM.Claim) until the VM’s state is written, so two devvm commands making or starting VMs at once never choose the same one. A build VM has no state, so devvm chooses its ssh port too, on every host, through the same allocator (ports.Allocator.Build), under the claims lock alone (state.Claims), and on macOS the build’s Seatbelt profile names that port. It records the port by the build VM’s name (run/build-ports/<name>), where ports.Used reads it, until limactl start returns, and by then Lima has bound the port or the start has failed. The devvm that starts the build holds a file lock on that record until then, and the kernel lets go of the lock when that devvm ends, even when it’s killed. Each time devvm chooses a port, under the claims lock, it first deletes the records whose lock no process holds and that are over 15 minutes old. The age matters because a killed devvm leaves its limactl start running, which may still bind the port for up to Lima’s 10 minutes of waiting for the VM’s ssh. So a devvm killed while its build VM starts reserves that port for 15 minutes, and then only until the next port is chosen. A stopped VM gets a new one only when a program on the host has its port on any address, even one that accepts no connections, or when the VM lists it to forward, and its start then sets it with an edit. Lima binds the port only once the VM boots, a few seconds after its start, so a port Lima picked itself would be free for another VM’s forwarder in that window, and Lima’s own ssh, which checks no host key, would then reach the other VM (the threat check below).
  • The host key. devvm keeps one record of a VM’s host keys for each of its starts, vms/<hash>/run/known_hosts (vmssh.PinHostKeys). It removes the record before each start and reads the keys after it, through limactl shell, at most 64 KiB for at most 30 s, keeping only lines whose key decodes and names its own type (vmssh.ParseHostKeys). The record’s first line names the start it was read for (backend.Run.ID), so a record of another start, such as one before a limactl start outside devvm, is read again, and keys read while the VM started again aren’t recorded. The forwarder checks the VM against that record, with HostKeyAlias and StrictHostKeyChecking yes, as the ssh config, links’ sessions and a --clone VM’s git do. All of them reach the VM through one function, vmssh.Checked, which checks the backend’s ssh and adds the record: the forwarder and the ssh config pin the keys when the record is another start’s, and links’ sessions and git take only a record of the current start. The pin keeps the forwarder from talking to a program on the host that takes the ssh port. It doesn’t guard against the VM itself, which is already the other end of the connection.
  • Its lifeline. The forwarder follows the hostagent’s pid file (ha.pid, the lifeline Lima’s Running gives), as the proxy does, and exits once the file is gone, holds anything else, or its process is gone. devvm stop stops it with the VM, and devvm rm and devvm gc --orphans stop it before they delete its files with the VM’s folder. A VM that stops some other way, such as when its self-check fails or a restart stops it, ends its forwarder through the lifeline, and the next start stops any forwarder that’s left before it starts its own.

What keeps a forward from carrying the VM out: every connection starts on the host. A program connects to the forwarder’s port, and the forwarder asks the VM’s sshd to connect to the VM’s loopback. The VM opens nothing to the host through the forwarder, because the master asks for no remote forward, agent, X11 or tunnel, and OpenSSH’s client refuses a channel that the server opens unasked, whatever sshd root in the VM runs. The only remote forwards devvm asks a VM for are a client’s links, on a link session that is a connection of its own, never the forwarder’s master (links). What the VM sends back goes to the program that connected, as with any forward. On a confined tier, the VM’s own connections stay confined by Seatbelt or QEMU’s restrict=on, while the forwarder runs on the host as devvm, outside the hostagent’s sandbox.

What it relies on: OpenSSH’s client refusing unrequested channels and honoring -F none, the kernel refusing a bind without SO_REUSEADDR where another socket has the port (checked on macOS), and devvm’s state listing every VM’s ports. It also relies on Lima binding its ssh forward on the host’s loopback alone, on the host key that devvm pins at the start, and on Lima honoring the ignore rules ahead of its own rule. On macOS, a confined VM relies on Seatbelt refusing the hostagent’s binds instead of on the rules, and on the Virtualization framework’s own process, which runs outside the profile, binding nothing: the VM’s network goes through the hostagent’s unix sockets.

What could break it: a Lima release that forwards despite the ignore rules, or that forwards from somewhere other than portForwards. On macOS, a confined VM keeps the guarantee even then, because its sandbox refuses the binds. An open VM, and every VM on Linux, where QEMU’s restrict=on doesn’t cover the hostagent’s own binds, still relies on Lima honoring the rules. A Lima release that needs a new bind for a confined VM, such as a resolver that can’t be turned off, fails its start closed, and Lima’s log names the refused bind. The end-to-end checks look at the rules, and use lsof or ss to check that the hostagent has no TCP or UDP port of the VM’s and that a host program keeps its port. A program on the host could take Lima’s ssh port while the VM is stopped, and the pinned host key refuses it. Lima’s key logs in to every VM in devvm’s Lima home, as it does for Lima’s own ssh, but public key authentication never sends the key to the VM.

Threat check (the security-audit skill, guidance mode, its local IPC companion; the sandbox’s binds and the ssh port). Leads, each confirmed and fixed, ruled out, or listed:

  • Another VM answering for this one’s ssh: confirmed, fixed. An ssh port that Lima picks at a VM’s start, and binds once the VM boots, is one devvm doesn’t record, so no forwarder reserves it. Another VM forwarding every port, with a server on that port in the window, has its forward take it. Lima then carries on with its other ssh forward and waits on the port (seen with a host program holding it), and Lima’s own ssh checks no host key (StrictHostKeyChecking no), so limactl shell, the host keys devvm reads and pins after the start, and devvm’s setup and shell would reach the other VM. The fix: each VM’s ssh port is devvm’s, whatever its tier, recorded before the clone and reserved by every forwarder. It’s unit-tested and checked by the CLI tests, and end to end, the port a VM’s state records is the one Lima listens on.
  • A guest port bound around the rules: ruled out on macOS on a confined tier. Lima forwards a port only by binding it on the host, and the sandbox refuses every port but the ssh port. End to end, with Lima’s own rule put back for one start inside the sandbox, Lima tries the guest’s TCP and UDP ports, is refused (operation not permitted), and has no port but its ssh port, while devvm’s forwarder forwards the TCP port.
  • The ssh port on every address: listed. Seatbelt allows the ssh port on any address, so a Lima that bound it on 0.0.0.0 would put the VM’s sshd on the network, where it still takes only keys. Lima binds it on 127.0.0.1, and the end-to-end checks look at the hostagent’s listeners. The rule allows the port over TCP alone, so the guest’s UDP server on that port number can’t get a forward from it; checked end to end.
  • A program holding a stopped VM’s ssh port: ruled out, but for a race. A start looks for the recorded port with a bind on 127.0.0.1 and ::1 as well as a connection, so a program that has the port on any address, even one that accepts no connections, gives the VM a new port. Only a program that takes the port between that check and Lima’s bind, a few seconds later, gets Lima’s ssh, which is listed under not covered below. End to end, a VM whose port a host program holds starts on a new one, recorded, and the program keeps its own.
  • Two VMs choosing the same ssh port: confirmed, fixed. Without a lock, two devvm commands making VMs at once could each choose the same port from the ports other VMs record, and the second VM’s Lima would wait on a port that the first one’s has. devvm chooses and records a port while it holds the claims lock, run/claims.lock in its data folder, after the VM’s own lock (locks).
  • A build VM’s ssh port: confirmed, fixed. A port that Lima picked at a build’s start would be one that no VM’s state records, so another VM forwarding every port could take it in the window before Lima binds it, and Lima’s ssh would then run the build’s scripts in that VM. The fix: devvm chooses every build VM’s ssh port, on macOS and Linux, under the claims lock, and records it in run/build-ports/<name>, which every forwarder reserves, until the build VM’s start returns. A record that a killed devvm leaves is deleted the first time devvm chooses a port once the record is 15 minutes old, because no process holds its lock, and until then it keeps the port from any VM while the start that the killed devvm left may still bind it. Builds carry no credentials, an image is the build VM’s own disk, and a tool build writes its images through a folder that only its own VM mounts, so even a VM that reached a build’s ssh another way could break that build but couldn’t learn a secret from it or choose what an image or a tool image holds. It’s unit-tested on both systems, and the CLI tests check that a build’s start sets the port.
  • What a failed start or create leaves: ruled out. A VM whose create fails, other than by an interrupt, keeps its state, and with it its recorded port, until devvm rm deletes it, so the port stays reserved and nothing else takes it. devvm rm deletes the state, which frees the port.
  • Unix sockets: ruled out as a way out. The hostagent binds them only in the VM’s Lima folder, which only Lima’s own commands and devvm use.
  • DNS around the proxy: ruled out. With Lima’s resolver off, the guest’s DNS server is 127.0.0.1, which transparent mode’s dnsmasq answers inside the VM with one stand-in address and no upstream, or nothing answers when it’s off, and Lima’s network’s DNS address and the host’s address on it answer nothing even when root asks them directly with transparent mode stopped, because the sandbox denies the hostagent the host’s DNS service and every connection but the proxy’s; checked end to end, with transparent mode stopped and running.
  • A compromised hostagent: listed. The bind rules stop a Lima that misbehaves, not code an attacker runs in it, which the profile still lets read and write your files.
  • Starts without the sandbox: listed. Only confined starts on macOS run under it. A build keeps Lima’s host resolver, so its binds aren’t denied, and an open VM starts unconfined. Such a VM could run under a profile that denies binds alone, as its ssh port is fixed, but it would need Lima’s resolver off too, which changes how it resolves names (the user-mode network’s own DNS instead of the host’s resolver), so that’s proposed rather than done.

Threat check for listed ports (the security-audit skill, its local IPC companion). Listed ports use the same forwarder with -only, so these leads are what listed ports add, each confirmed or ruled out:

  • A port the VM chooses: ruled out. -only comes from the VM’s state, less the ports a host program has, both read on the host by the forwarder’s owner, and the VM’s reports can’t add to it. A listed port is forwarded only while a server in the VM listens on it, as with every port.
  • Port 22 listed: ruled out as a collision. Port 22 in the VM is its sshd, and Lima’s ssh forward comes from another host port, so a listed 22 forwards the VM’s sshd to the host’s port 22 as it would forward any server. The VM’s sshd still takes only keys. A host whose own sshd has port 22 keeps it, with a ports_taken warning.
  • A listed proxy port: ruled out. The forwarder reserves the VM’s own proxy port whether or not it’s listed, and every other VM’s as well.
  • A listed port below 1024: taken because the user asked for it. A host service that has the port keeps it, and a bind the host refuses is logged. One that isn’t running yet is under Not covered.
  • A forwarder left behind: ruled out. devvm stop stops it, devvm rm stops it and removes its files, any other stop ends it through its lifeline, and a start or change whose listed ports are all taken runs none. Two devvm runs that start a VM’s forwarder at once take turns on the VM’s lock, so the second stops the first one’s forwarder, and neither leaves one that its pid file doesn’t name, which nothing would stop.
  • A tier’s confinement: ruled out. Listed ports take fewer ports than every port, never more, and every connection still starts on the host.

Not covered:

  • A VM can take a free port from 1024 up, or a listed one, on the host’s loopback that a program there expects to be its own, such as one that isn’t running yet or is restarting. What the VM serves there reaches whatever connects, so a page it serves to the user’s browser can reach the internet from the host, past the VM’s tier.
  • A host program that starts on a port while the VM has it forwarded still binds it when it listens on all addresses with SO_REUSEADDR, as most servers do (checked on macOS). Its loopback connections then reach the VM, because the forward’s address is the narrower one. A program that binds without SO_REUSEADDR is refused.
  • The VM can make the forwarder dial a host loopback port that’s in use and then close the connection at once without sending anything, because that’s how the forwarder checks for a port held only by ended connections. This happens at most once per port every second, as the VM’s listener on the port goes and comes back.
  • Servers only on the VM’s other addresses, such as its network address or a container’s, aren’t forwarded.
  • Other users on the host reach the forwards, because they’re on the host’s loopback.
  • UDP isn’t forwarded. Ports shows how to tunnel it over TCP.
  • A server that keeps a port while its forward couldn’t be made, because the host had the port, isn’t forwarded until it stops and starts again.
  • Another user on the host can take a VM’s ssh port while the VM is stopped or booting. Lima’s own ssh would then reach that user’s program, as it checks no host key, while devvm’s forwarder and ssh config pin the VM’s.
  • A VM started outside devvm, such as with devvm limactl start, or one whose forwarder ended, runs without forwarded ports until its next start through devvm, or until devvm ports changes its ports, which starts a forwarder with the host key devvm pinned at its last start.

End-to-end checks (tests/e2e, project, and network for the sandbox’s binds):
